claim: Sound location in the horizontal plane is decoded from the relative summed activity of two populations in each hemisphere according to a recent theory.
source: In the auditory brainstem, a recent theory proposes that sound location in the horizontal plane is decoded from the relative summed activity of two populations in each hemisphere, whereas earlier theories hypothesized that the location was decoded from the identity of the most active cells.
evidence: This is cited as a recent theory in the field, representing established scientific discourse.

claim: Earlier theories hypothesized that sound location was decoded from the identity of the most active cells.
source: In the auditory brainstem, a recent theory proposes that sound location in the horizontal plane is decoded from the relative summed activity of two populations in each hemisphere, whereas earlier theories hypothesized that the location was decoded from the identity of the most active cells.
evidence: This refers to earlier theories in the field, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: There is insufficient information in the pooled activity of each hemisphere to estimate sound direction in a reliable way consistent with behavior.
source: We demonstrate that there is insufficient information in the pooled activity of each hemisphere to estimate sound direction in a reliable way consistent with behavior, whereas robust estimates can be obtained from neural activity by taking into account the heterogeneous tuning of cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the decoder performance analysis presented in the results.

claim: Robust estimates of sound direction can be obtained from neural activity by taking into account the heterogeneous tuning of cells.
source: We demonstrate that there is insufficient information in the pooled activity of each hemisphere to estimate sound direction in a reliable way consistent with behavior, whereas robust estimates can be obtained from neural activity by taking into account the heterogeneous tuning of cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: Robust estimates of sound direction can be obtained when only contralateral neural responses are used, consistently with unilateral lesion studies.
source: These estimates can still be obtained when only contralateral neural responses are used, consistently with unilateral lesion studies.
evidence: This is supported by the lesion simulation results in Figure 7B and comparison with cited lesion studies.

claim: Humans and many other species use submillisecond timing differences in the signals arriving at the two ears to localize sound sources in the horizontal plane.
source: To localize sound sources in the horizontal plane, humans and many other species use submillisecond timing differences in the signals arriving at the two ears (Ashida and Carr, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ashida and Carr, 2011.

claim: The ear closer to the sound source receives the sound earlier than the other ear.
source: The ear closer to the source receives the sound earlier than the other.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sound propagation and interaural time differences.

claim: Interaural time differences (ITDs) are encoded in the auditory brainstem by binaural neurons, which are tuned to both frequency and ITD.
source: These interaural time differences (ITDs) are encoded in the auditory brainstem by binaural neurons, which are tuned to both frequency and ITD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory neuroscience.

claim: An influential theory proposes that ITD is represented by the activity pattern of cells with heterogeneous tunings, a pattern code for sound location.
source: An influential theory proposes that ITD is represented by the activity pattern of cells with heterogeneous tunings, a pattern code for sound location (Jeffress, 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeffress, 1948.

claim: In a stronger version of the Jeffress theory, ITD is represented by the identity of the most active cell in each frequency band, a labeled line code for sound location.
source: In a stronger version, ITD is represented by the identity of the most active cell in each frequency band, a labeled line code for sound location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Jeffress theory presented as established knowledge.

claim: The Jeffress theory has proved successful in barn owls.
source: Although this theory has proved successful in barn owls (Konishi, 2003), discrepancies have been observed in mammals.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Konishi, 2003.

claim: Discrepancies with the Jeffress theory have been observed in mammals.
source: Although this theory has proved successful in barn owls (Konishi, 2003), discrepancies have been observed in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the field, implicitly supported by subsequent citations.

claim: At low frequencies, many cells have best delays (BDs) larger than the physiological range of ITDs experienced by the animal in mammals.
source: In particular, at low frequencies, many cells have best delays (BDs) larger than the physiological range of ITDs experienced by the animal (McAlpine et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McAlpine et al., 2001.

claim: In a labeled line code, cells with best delays larger than the physiological range would not have any function.
source: In a labeled line code, these cells would not have any function.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the labeled line code.

claim: An alternative theory proposes that ITD is coded not by the firing of individual cells, but by the relative summed activity of each hemisphere, a summation code for sound location.
source: An alternative theory was proposed, in which ITD is coded not by the firing of individual cells, but by the relative summed activity of each hemisphere, a summation code for sound location (Stecker et al., 2005; Grothe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stecker et al., 2005 and Grothe et al., 2010.

claim: The nature of the neural code for ITD in mammals is still contentious because it is not known whether the auditory system sums activity or uses cell identity in decoding responses.
source: The nature of the neural code for ITD in mammals is still contentious because it is not known whether the auditory system sums activity or uses cell identity in decoding responses.
evidence: This is stated as the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cells with large BDs maximize ITD sensitivity of firing rate in the physiological range.
source: In favor of the summation code hypothesis, cells with large BDs maximize ITD sensitivity of firing rate in the physiological range, whereas they are useless in a labeled line code.
evidence: This is stated as an argument in favor of the summation code, representing established knowledge.

claim: Most of the cells with BDs inside the physiological range actually degrade a summation code because their rates do not vary monotonically with ITD.
source: However, most of the cells with BDs inside the physiological range (most cells in cats; Kuwada and Yin, 1983; Yin and Chan, 1990a) actually degrade a summation code because their rates do not vary monotonically with ITD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuwada and Yin, 1983 and Yin and Chan, 1990a.

claim: Most cells in cats have BDs inside the physiological range.
source: However, most of the cells with BDs inside the physiological range (most cells in cats; Kuwada and Yin, 1983; Yin and Chan, 1990a) actually degrade a summation code because their rates do not vary monotonically with ITD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuwada and Yin, 1983 and Yin and Chan, 1990a.

claim: In simple situations where there is a single acoustical stimulus with unknown ITD, theoretical arguments show that a summation code is optimal at low frequencies.
source: In simple situations where there is a single acoustical stimulus (e.g., tone) with unknown ITD, theoretical arguments show that a summation code is optimal at low frequencies (Harper and McAlpine, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harper and McAlpine, 2004.

claim: With simple stimuli, taking into account cell identity rather than simply summing all responses does not improve performance.
source: Previous studies have also shown that with simple stimuli, taking into account cell identity rather than simply summing all responses does not improve performance (Lesica et al., 2010; Lüling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lesica et al., 2010 and Lüling et al., 2011.

claim: What is optimal in a simple world may not be optimal in an ecological environment.
source: However, what is optimal in a simple world may not be optimal in an ecological environment.
evidence: This is a general theoretical principle stated by the authors.

claim: In a simple situation where only the ITD varies, the optimal code is the most sensitive one.
source: In a simple situation where only the ITD varies, the optimal code is the most sensitive one.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle.

claim: In complex situations where other dimensions also vary, there is a trade-off between sensitivity and robustness, so the optimal code is not the most sensitive one.
source: In complex situations where other dimensions also vary, there is a trade-off between sensitivity and robustness, so the optimal code is not the most sensitive one (Brette, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brette, 2010.

claim: Theory predicts that in complex situations, the heterogeneity of ITD tunings is critical to produce robust estimates.
source: In fact, theory predicts that in complex situations, the heterogeneity of ITD tunings is critical to produce robust estimates.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction, implicitly supported by the citation to Brette, 2010.

claim: Summing cell responses is strongly suboptimal in complex situations.
source: We found that summing cell responses is strongly suboptimal and that heterogeneity in tunings is information rather than noise.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity in tunings is information rather than noise.
source: We found that summing cell responses is strongly suboptimal and that heterogeneity in tunings is information rather than noise.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the decoder performance analysis, particularly Figure 7A.

claim: The peak decoder performs poorly because of the noise in spiking.
source: We observe already that although we chose cells with BFs in a narrow frequency band (640–760 Hz), the peak decoder performs poorly because of the noise in spiking.
evidence: This is an observation from the model results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The smoothed peak decoder is less noisy than the peak decoder.
source: This decoder is less noisy.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the smoothed peak decoder compared to the peak decoder.

claim: The hemispheric difference varies systematically with ITD.
source: This gives a value between −1 and 1, the hemispheric difference, which varies systematically with ITD (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A, right panel.

claim: The relationship between hemispheric difference and ITD depends on the frequency band in which the hemispheric difference is computed.
source: Note, however, that this relationship depends on the frequency band in which the hemispheric difference is computed.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A, right panel, showing different curves for different frequencies.

claim: At high best frequencies (around 1300 Hz), ambiguities occur in the hemispheric decoder where a single hemispheric difference value is consistent with multiple ITDs.
source: More importantly, ambiguities start to occur at these high BFs: for example, a hemispheric difference of −0.8 is consistent with ITDs of both 100 and 300 µs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A, right panel, for the purple curve at 1300 Hz.

claim: Ambiguities in the hemispheric decoder occur when the physiological range of ITD represents more than one period of the auditory filter's center frequency.
source: This occurs when the physiological range of ITD represents more than one period of the auditory filter's center frequency.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the ambiguities observed in the hemispheric decoder.

claim: The hemispheric decoder performs better than both the peak and smoothed peak decoders for the guinea pig model at all frequencies.
source: The hemispheric decoder performs better than both decoders for the guinea pig model at all frequencies, but for the cat, it is only better than the smoothed peak decoder for frequencies below 600 Hz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B for the guinea pig model.

claim: For the cat model, the hemispheric decoder is only better than the smoothed peak decoder for frequencies below 600 Hz.
source: The hemispheric decoder performs better than both decoders for the guinea pig model at all frequencies, but for the cat, it is only better than the smoothed peak decoder for frequencies below 600 Hz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B for the cat model.

claim: The hemispheric decoder is a very poor decoder of ITD for the cat model, except at very low frequency.
source: Thus, it appears that even for this simple scenario, the hemispheric decoder is a very poor decoder of ITD for the cat model, except at very low frequency.
evidence: This is an inference from the results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The estimation error of the hemispheric decoder starts increasing at a lower frequency for the cat than for the guinea pig model due to the larger head size of the cat.
source: The fact that the estimation error of the hemispheric decoder starts increasing at a lower frequency for the cat than for the guinea pig model was expected based on the larger head size of the cat (Harper and McAlpine, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harper and McAlpine, 2004 and the data in Figure 2B.

claim: The peak decoder selects a single cell, so its estimation error reflects the level of noise in individual responses, which is high.
source: Because the peak decoder selects a single cell, its estimation error reflects the level of noise in individual responses, which is high.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the poor performance of the peak decoder.

claim: The smoothed decoder improves on the peak decoder but still mostly uses the responses of cells with similar tuning.
source: The smoothed decoder improves on this matter, but still mostly uses the responses of cells with similar tuning.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the limitations of the smoothed decoder.

claim: At low frequencies, both the peak and smoothed peak estimators rely on the responses of a small pool of cells with BDs inside the physiological range.
source: In addition, at low frequencies, both estimators rely on the responses of a small pool of cells with BDs inside the physiological range.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the limitations of these decoders.

claim: The hemispheric decoder sums all responses, which reduces noise but also discards all information about BF and BD.
source: The hemispheric decoder sums all responses, which reduces noise but also discards all information about BF and BD.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the limitations of the hemispheric decoder.

claim: The pattern match decoder can be implemented by a single-layer neural network in which the output neurons encode the preferred ITD and the synaptic weights represent the patterns.
source: This can be implemented by a single-layer neural network in which the output neurons encode the preferred ITD and the synaptic weights represent the patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a description of how the pattern match decoder could be neurally implemented, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pattern match decoder performs better than both the peak and hemispheric decoders for both the guinea pig and cat models.
source: The pattern match decoder performs better than both the other decoders, both for the guinea pig and the cat models.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in performance between the pattern match decoder and the hemispheric decoder is very large for the cat model.
source: The difference with the hemispheric decoder is very large for the cat model, but for the guinea pig model, it only starts being substantial above 1 kHz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For the guinea pig model, the difference between the pattern match decoder and the hemispheric decoder only starts being substantial above 1 kHz.
source: The difference with the hemispheric decoder is very large for the cat model, but for the guinea pig model, it only starts being substantial above 1 kHz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The pattern match decoder combines the advantages of the hemispheric and peak decoders: it averages spiking noise over all cells, but it still uses individual information about BF and BD.
source: The pattern match decoder combines the advantages of the hemispheric and peak decoders: it averages spiking noise over all cells, but it still uses individual information about BF and BD.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why the pattern match decoder performs well.

claim: The pattern match decoder outperformed several other standard decoders from machine learning, including optimal linear decoding, maximum likelihood estimation, and nearest neighbor regression.
source: We also tested several other standard decoders from machine learning, including optimal linear decoding, maximum likelihood estimation, and nearest neighbor regression, but the pattern match decoder outperformed them in all cases and so we do not present the results of these decoders here (although see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for a sample of these results).
evidence: This is stated as a result of testing multiple decoders, with data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the guinea pig model, the error made by the pattern match decoder is about half the error of the hemispheric decoder when integrating information across frequency.
source: For this more realistic task, it appears that the error made by the pattern match decoder is about half the error of the hemispheric decoder for the guinea pig model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the cat model, the difference in performance between the pattern match decoder and the hemispheric decoder is even larger than for the guinea pig model when integrating information across frequency.
source: For the cat models, this difference is even larger.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the cat, the smoothed peak decoder performs better than the hemispheric decoder when integrating information across frequency.
source: In fact, it turns out that for the cat, the smoothed peak decoder performs better than the hemispheric decoder.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All decoders perform much worse when trained on broadband noise and tested on band-pass noise than when trained and tested in the same frequency bands.
source: First, all decoders perform much worse than when decoders are trained and tested in the same frequency bands (compare with Figure 2B; the unsmoothed peak decoder performs very poorly and is not shown).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 3B with Figure 2B.

claim: Frequency integration is an issue for all decoders.
source: This means that frequency integration is indeed an issue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all decoders perform worse when tested across frequencies.

claim: The hemispheric decoder performs worse than the peak and smoothed peak decoders above 700 Hz for the guinea pig model and above 500 Hz for the cat when trained on broadband noise and tested on band-pass noise.
source: Second, the hemispheric decoder performs worse than the two other decoders above 700 Hz for the guinea pig models and above 500 Hz for the cat.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The hemispheric difference is ambiguous at high frequency (above about 1200 Hz for both guinea pig and cat).
source: This was expected for two reasons: (1) the hemispheric difference is ambiguous at high frequency (above about 1200 Hz for both animals), and (2) the hemispheric difference depends not only on ITD but also on frequency (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the poor performance of the hemispheric decoder at high frequencies.

claim: The hemispheric difference depends not only on ITD but also on frequency.
source: This was expected for two reasons: (1) the hemispheric difference is ambiguous at high frequency (above about 1200 Hz for both animals), and (2) the hemispheric difference depends not only on ITD but also on frequency (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A, right panel.

claim: For both the guinea pig and cat models, the error of the hemispheric decoder starts increasing when cells with BF above 1.2 kHz are included.
source: Both for the guinea pig and the cat models, the error of the hemispheric decoder starts increasing when cells with BF above 1.2 kHz are included.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The error of the pattern match decoder continues decreasing as cells with high frequency are added.
source: We note, however, that the error of the pattern match decoder continues decreasing as cells with high frequency are added.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The hemispheric decoder is not robust to changes in spectrum.
source: The hemispheric decoder is not robust to changes in spectrum, as the error increases with noise color α.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: As noise color α increases, the estimate of the ITD by the hemispheric decoder becomes more and more biased to the center.
source: As α increases, the estimate of the ITD becomes more and more biased to the center.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D, bottom panel.

claim: With high α, every cell receives more low frequencies than high frequencies compared to the white noise case, and therefore the hemispheric difference curve changes and becomes flatter.
source: This is because with high α, every cell receives more low frequencies than high frequencies compared to the white noise case, and therefore the hemispheric difference curve changes and becomes flatter (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the bias in the hemispheric decoder with colored noise.

claim: The ITD tuning curves have different shapes, depending on the cell's BF.
source: The ITD tuning curves have different shapes, depending on the cell's BF (left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, left panel.

claim: The hemispheric difference in each frequency band varies with the center frequency.
source: As a result, the hemispheric difference in each frequency band varies with the center frequency (middle).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, middle panel.

claim: The hemispheric difference curves are shallower in low frequency and sharper in high frequency.
source: The curves are shallower in low frequency and sharper in high frequency (right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, right panel.

claim: The slope of the hemispheric difference is expected to be proportional to frequency because the hemispheric difference is determined by the interaural phase difference, which is the product of frequency and ITD.
source: In fact, the slope is expected to be proportional to frequency: the hemispheric difference is determined by the interaural phase difference, which is the product of frequency and ITD.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation for the frequency dependence of the hemispheric difference.

claim: Normalizing the cell responses by their BF in the calculation of the hemispheric difference produces hemispheric differences with similar slopes in all frequency bands.
source: Therefore, we fix this issue by normalizing the cell responses by their BF in the calculation of the hemispheric difference ('Materials and methods'). This produces hemispheric differences with similar slopes in all frequency bands.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, right panel.

claim: The frequency-dependent correction improves ITD estimation for the hemispheric decoder when the decoder is trained on broadband noise and tested on band-passed noise.
source: This frequency-dependent correction indeed improves ITD estimation when the decoder is trained on broadband noise and on band-passed noise (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The error of the frequency-dependent hemispheric decoder still remains higher than in the simple case when the decoder is trained and tested in the same frequency band.
source: However, the error still remains higher than in the simple case when the decoder is trained and tested in the same frequency band.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B by comparing with the dotted lines.

claim: The frequency-dependent correction improves the performance of the pattern match decoder above 600 Hz, where it is close to the performance obtained in the simple case.
source: In the same way, we improved frequency integration for the pattern match decoder by calculating intermediate estimates in each frequency band and combining the results ('Materials and methods'). This correction improves the performance above 600 Hz, where it is close to the performance obtained in the simple case.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In all cases, the pattern match decoder performs best when background noise is added.
source: In all cases, the pattern match decoder performs best, but for the guinea pig models, it substantially outperforms the hemispheric decoder at low SNR, whereas it showed similar performance in quiet.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For the guinea pig model, the pattern match decoder substantially outperforms the hemispheric decoder at low SNR, whereas it showed similar performance in quiet.
source: In all cases, the pattern match decoder performs best, but for the guinea pig models, it substantially outperforms the hemispheric decoder at low SNR, whereas it showed similar performance in quiet.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The smoothed peak decoder outperforms the hemispheric decoder at SNR below 10 dB, both for the guinea pig and the cat models.
source: Interestingly, the smoothed peak decoder also outperforms the hemispheric decoder at SNR below 10 dB, both for the guinea pig and the cat models.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Although the smoothed peak decoder performs worst in quiet, it proves more robust than the hemispheric decoder in noise.
source: Indeed, although this decoder performs worst in quiet, it proves more robust than the hemispheric decoder.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The poor performance of the hemispheric decoder in noise can be accounted for by a bias problem.
source: The poor performance of the hemispheric decoder can again be accounted for by a bias problem.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B, right column.

claim: At high SNR, the hemispheric difference curves become shallower, which implies that ITD estimation is biased toward the center.
source: At high SNR, the hemispheric difference curves become shallower, which implies that ITD estimation is biased toward the center.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the bias in the hemispheric decoder at low SNR.

claim: The smoothed peak decoder tends to be biased away from the center.
source: Note that the smoothed peak decoder tends to be biased away from the center.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B, right column.

claim: The smoothed peak decoder is biased away from the center because BDs are more represented away from the center.
source: This is simply because BDs are more represented away from the center.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the bias in the smoothed peak decoder.

claim: Sounds are diffracted by the head in reality, not simply delayed.
source: Previously, we considered a simplistic model of sound propagation, in which sounds are simply delayed. In reality, sounds are diffracted by the head.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sound propagation.

claim: A better description of sound propagation is that sounds arriving at the two ears are two filtered versions of the original sound, with filters depending on source direction.
source: A better description of this process is that sounds arriving at the two ears are two filtered versions of the original sound, with filters depending on source direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HRTFs.

claim: Diffraction produces ITDs that depend on frequency for the same source direction, with larger ITDs in low frequency.
source: It is known that diffraction produces ITDs that depend on frequency for the same source direction, with larger ITDs in low frequency (Kuhn, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuhn, 1977.

claim: The measured guinea pig HRTFs show the same pattern of frequency-dependent ITDs as previously reported, with larger ITDs in low frequency.
source: We find the same pattern in our measurements (Figure 6B), and the range of ITDs is similar to previously reported measurements in live guinea pigs (Sterbing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and supported by citation to Sterbing et al., 2003.

claim: For both guinea pig and cat, the pattern match decoder is substantially better than the hemispheric decoder when using HRTFs.
source: For both animals, the pattern match decoder is substantially better than the hemispheric decoder.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Since the hemispheric decoder discards all information about BF and BD, it cannot take advantage of the frequency variation of ITDs, whereas the pattern match decoder does.
source: Indeed, since the hemispheric decoder discards all information about BF and BD, it cannot take advantage of the frequency variation of ITDs, whereas the pattern match decoder does.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the superior performance of the pattern match decoder with HRTFs.

claim: The difference in performance between the pattern match and hemispheric decoders is particularly striking for the cat due to its larger head size.
source: The difference is particularly striking for the cat due to its larger head size.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and explained by the larger frequency-dependent ITD variations in cats.

claim: When the BDs are less heterogeneous, there is little difference between the performance of the hemispheric and pattern match decoder.
source: When the BDs are less heterogeneous, there is little difference between the performance of the hemispheric and pattern match decoder.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: As heterogeneity increases, the pattern match decoder performs better, whereas the hemispheric decoder shows little change in performance.
source: But as heterogeneity increases, the pattern match decoder performs better, whereas the hemispheric decoder shows little change in performance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Heterogeneity of tunings is useful to estimate the ITD, and pooling the responses discards this information.
source: Therefore, heterogeneity of tunings is indeed useful to estimate the ITD, and pooling the responses discards this information.
evidence: This is inferred from the results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Performance of the pattern match decoder remains stable when the distribution is made more heterogeneous than the actual distribution (spread factor >1).
source: Performance remains stable when the distribution is made more heterogeneous than the actual distribution (spread factor >1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Lesion studies in cats show that when one inferior colliculus is removed, the sound localization performance in the contralateral field drops but remains almost intact in the ipsilateral field.
source: Lesion studies in cats (Jenkins and Masterton, 1982) and in humans (Litovsky et al., 2002) show that when one inferior colliculus is removed, the sound localization performance in the contralateral field drops but remains almost intact in the ipsilateral field.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jenkins and Masterton, 1982 and Litovsky et al., 2002.

claim: Lesion studies in humans show that when one inferior colliculus is removed, the sound localization performance in the contralateral field drops but remains almost intact in the ipsilateral field.
source: Lesion studies in cats (Jenkins and Masterton, 1982) and in humans (Litovsky et al., 2002) show that when one inferior colliculus is removed, the sound localization performance in the contralateral field drops but remains almost intact in the ipsilateral field.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jenkins and Masterton, 1982 and Litovsky et al., 2002.

claim: The lesion study results are not compatible with an ITD estimation based on the comparison between the activity of the two hemispheres.
source: This is not compatible with an ITD estimation based on the comparison between the activity of the two hemispheres.
evidence: This is an inference from the lesion study results.

claim: After simulated hemispheric lesion, the performance of the pattern match decoder for positive ITDs is essentially unchanged, whereas it is highly degraded for negative ITDs.
source: The performance for positive ITDs is essentially unchanged, whereas it is highly degraded for negative ITDs, especially for the smoothed peak decoder.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Lesion data indicate that sound localization performance is greatly degraded in the contralateral hemifield, but not completely abolished.
source: Lesion data indicate that sound localization performance is greatly degraded in the contralateral hemifield, but not completely abolished, which would discard the smoothed peak decoder—although lesions might not have been complete, and those were free-field experiments involving other cues than ITD.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of lesion data.

claim: Barn owls are sensitive to ITDs in very high frequency (about 2–8 kHz).
source: Barn owls are sensitive to ITDs in very high frequency (about 2–8 kHz), and therefore, as expected, the hemispheric decoder performs very badly compared to the pattern match decoder (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about barn owl auditory processing.

claim: The hemispheric decoder performs very badly compared to the pattern match decoder for barn owls.
source: Barn owls are sensitive to ITDs in very high frequency (about 2–8 kHz), and therefore, as expected, the hemispheric decoder performs very badly compared to the pattern match decoder (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: For humans, the distribution of BD vs BF is unknown.
source: For humans, the distribution of BD vs BF is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as the current state of knowledge.

claim: Some indirect evidence from MRI and EEG studies suggests that BD is not uniformly distributed in humans.
source: Some indirect evidence from MRI and EEG studies suggests that BD is not uniformly distributed (Thompson et al., 2006; Briley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2006 and Briley et al., 2013.

claim: In all tested cases for humans, the estimation error of the hemispheric decoder is very high, an order of magnitude larger than human sound localization acuity (on the order of 3°).
source: In all cases, the estimation error of the hemispheric decoder is very high, an order of magnitude larger than human sound localization acuity (on the order of 3°) (Carlile et al., 1997).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B-D and compared with behavioral data from Carlile et al., 1997.

claim: Human sound localization acuity is on the order of 3°.
source: In all cases, the estimation error of the hemispheric decoder is very high, an order of magnitude larger than human sound localization acuity (on the order of 3°) (Carlile et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carlile et al., 1997.

claim: The performance obtained by a decoder in a given context is always overestimated, compared to the same decoder adapted to a more general context, even when tested with the same sounds.
source: Therefore, we must stress again that the performance obtained by a decoder in a given context is always overestimated, compared to the same decoder adapted to a more general context, 'even when tested with the same sounds'.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about decoder performance.

claim: All decoders are much more accurate when trained and tested on a single narrow frequency band than when trained with broadband sounds and tested with exactly the same narrowband sounds.
source: To give an example, all decoders are much more accurate when trained and tested on a single narrow frequency band (Figure 2B) than when trained with broadband sounds and tested with exactly the same narrowband sounds (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 2B and Figure 3B.

claim: A sound localization system adapted for the full range of ecological variability necessarily performs worse in a narrower range of conditions than a system specifically optimized for that narrow range.
source: A sound localization system adapted for the full range of ecological variability necessarily performs worse in a narrower range of conditions than a system specifically optimized for that narrow range.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about sensory systems.

claim: Sound localization acuity is constrained by the precision of the feedback mechanism that associates acoustical cues with sound location.
source: In addition, acoustical cues must be associated with sound location through some feedback mechanism, and therefore sound localization acuity is constrained by the precision of this feedback.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical consideration about sound localization.

claim: A comparative study across 23 mammalian species shows that sound localization acuity is best explained by the width of the field of best vision.
source: Indeed a comparative study across 23 mammalian species shows that sound localization acuity is best explained by the width of the field of best vision (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: The model results should be understood as a lower bound for the accuracy of these decoders.
source: Therefore, our model results should be understood as a lower bound for the accuracy of these decoders.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model results.

claim: The poor performance of the hemispheric decoder is actually optimistic, especially as specific efforts were made to enhance it by taking into account nonlinearities and by applying frequency-dependent corrections.
source: In particular, the poor performance of the hemispheric decoder is actually optimistic, all the more so as we made specific efforts to enhance it by taking into account nonlinearities (Figure 2A) and by applying frequency-dependent corrections (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: In cats, the minimum audible angle (MAA) is about 5° for broadband noises longer than 40 ms.
source: In cats, the MAA is about 5° for broadband noises longer than 40 ms (defined as the speaker separation given 75% correct responses) (Casseday and Neff, 1973; Heffner and Heffner, 1988a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casseday and Neff, 1973 and Heffner and Heffner, 1988a.

claim: In an absolute localization study in cats, when the cat's head is unrestrained, direction estimates show little bias and the standard deviation is 3–4°.
source: Tollin et al. (2005) measured accuracy in an absolute localization study in the −25° to 25° range. When the cat's head is unrestrained, direction estimates show little bias and the standard deviation is 3–4°, which corresponds to a mean unsigned error (the measure used in this article) of 2.4–3.2° (assuming normally distributed responses).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tollin et al., 2005.

claim: In Moore et al. (2008), the mean unsigned error for cats was in the 2–4° range for directions near the midline.
source: In Moore et al. (2008), the mean unsigned error was directly reported (although only for directions near the midline) and was in the 2–4° range.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moore et al., 2008.

claim: In a behavioral study where cats were trained to walk to a target speaker in the −90° to 90° range, the animals could do the task with nearly 100% accuracy, with no apparent dependence on speaker azimuth.
source: In a behavioral study in which cats were trained to walk to a target speaker in the −90° to 90° range, the animals could do the task with nearly 100% accuracy, with no apparent dependence on speaker azimuth (Malhotra et al., 2004)—but speakers were spaced by 15°.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malhotra et al., 2004.

claim: The mean unsigned error for the optimized hemispheric model in cats was 5° when trained and tested in quiet with broadband noises, with sources constrained to the horizontal plane.
source: In Figure 6D, we report a mean unsigned error of 5° for the optimized hemispheric model (including frequency-dependent and nonlinear corrections; error for the pattern decoder was nearly 0°).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Moore et al. (2008) showed for sources near the midline that sound localization accuracy in the horizontal plane is very similar for broadband and low-pass filtered noises (<5 kHz).
source: However, Moore et al. (2008) showed for sources near the midline that sound localization accuracy in the horizontal plane is very similar for broadband and low-pass filtered noises (<5 kHz), which do not include these cues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moore et al., 2008.

claim: In cats, the just noticeable difference in ITD is similar for tones of 500 Hz and 1 kHz, about 25 µs.
source: In cats, the just noticeable difference in ITD is similar for tones of 500 Hz and 1 kHz, about 25 µs (Wakeford and Robinson, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wakeford and Robinson, 1974.

claim: The performance of the pattern decoder is generally not strongly dependent on frequency in the 500–1200 Hz range.
source: The performance of the pattern decoder is generally not strongly dependent on frequency in the 500–1200 Hz range (Figures 2–4), whereas the performance of the hemispheric decoder consistently increases with frequency (between about 500 and 1 kHz in Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2–4.

claim: The performance of the hemispheric decoder consistently increases with frequency between about 500 and 1 kHz.
source: The performance of the pattern decoder is generally not strongly dependent on frequency in the 500–1200 Hz range (Figures 2–4), whereas the performance of the hemispheric decoder consistently increases with frequency (between about 500 and 1 kHz in Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the gerbil, the MAA is 27°.
source: In the gerbil, another small mammal with low-frequency hearing, the MAA is 27° (Heffner and Heffner, 1988b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1988b.

claim: Sound localization acuity in gerbils is one of the worst of all mammalian species in which it has been measured.
source: This makes sound localization acuity in gerbils one of the worst of all mammalian species in which it has been measured (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: The maximum ITD in gerbils is about 120 µs.
source: Given that the maximum ITD is about 120 µs (Maki and Furukawa, 2005), the threshold ITD should be about 54 µs (using Kuhn's formula; Kuhn, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maki and Furukawa, 2005.

claim: For a given accuracy, the hemispheric decoder requires many more neurons than the pattern match decoder.
source: We note however that, for a given accuracy, the hemispheric decoder requires many more neurons than the pattern match decoder (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In owls, ITD is a cue to azimuth, whereas interaural level difference is a cue to elevation.
source: In owls, ITD is a cue to azimuth, whereas interaural level difference is a cue to elevation (Takahashi et al., 1984; Moiseff, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 1984 and Moiseff, 1989.

claim: The mean unsigned error with the hemispheric decoder for barn owls was greater than 30° when trained and tested in quiet with HRTFs.
source: We found that the mean unsigned error with the hemispheric decoder was greater than 30°, when trained and tested in quiet with HRTFs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Behaviorally, barn owls localize broadband sounds with azimuthal error smaller than about 10° at all azimuths.
source: Behaviorally, barn owls localize broadband sounds with azimuthal error smaller than about 10° at all azimuths (Knudsen et al., 1979), and a large part of this error is due to an underestimate of eccentric azimuths that can be accounted for by a prior for frontal directions (Fischer and Peña, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knudsen et al., 1979 and Fischer and Peña, 2011.

claim: In humans, behavioral estimates of azimuth are largely dominated by low-frequency ITDs.
source: In humans, behavioral estimates of azimuth are largely dominated by low-frequency ITDs (Wightman and Kistler, 1992), and the mean unsigned error with broadband noise bursts (open-loop condition) is about 5° in the frontal hemifield (2–10° depending on azimuth) in a two-dimensional absolute localization task (Makous and Middlebrooks, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wightman and Kistler, 1992.

claim: In humans, the mean unsigned error with broadband noise bursts (open-loop condition) is about 5° in the frontal hemifield (2–10° depending on azimuth) in a two-dimensional absolute localization task.
source: In humans, behavioral estimates of azimuth are largely dominated by low-frequency ITDs (Wightman and Kistler, 1992), and the mean unsigned error with broadband noise bursts (open-loop condition) is about 5° in the frontal hemifield (2–10° depending on azimuth) in a two-dimensional absolute localization task (Makous and Middlebrooks, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makous and Middlebrooks, 1990.

claim: The hemispheric decoder has an average error of about 10° in the most favorable scenario for humans, although sources are constrained to the horizontal plane.
source: In contrast, the hemispheric decoder has an average error of about 10° in the most favorable scenario (Figure 8B), although sources are constrained to the horizontal plane.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The results with the hemispheric decoder appear inconsistent with behavioral data for cats, humans, and owls.
source: In summary, our results with the hemispheric decoder appear inconsistent with behavioral data for cats, humans, and owls.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparing model results with behavioral data.

claim: The results obtained by the pattern match decoder imply that there is enough information in the activity of binaural neurons to account for the sound localization accuracy of cats, humans, and owls.
source: In contrast, the results obtained by the pattern match decoder imply that there is enough information in the activity of binaural neurons to account for the sound localization accuracy of these species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparing model results with behavioral data.

claim: There is insufficient behavioral data in the guinea pig model to distinguish between different decoders.
source: There is insufficient behavioral data in the guinea pig model to distinguish between different decoders.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in comparing model results with behavioral data.

claim: The Jeffress theory asserts that ITD is represented in the activity pattern of neurons with heterogeneous tunings to ITD.
source: One theory, initially proposed by Jeffress (1948), asserts that ITD is represented in the activity pattern of neurons with heterogeneous tunings to ITD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeffress, 1948.

claim: A more recent theory claims that ITD is represented by the relative activity of the two MSOs, irrespective of the tunings of the cells.
source: A more recent theory claims that ITD is represented by the relative activity of the two MSOs, irrespective of the tunings of the cells (Grothe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grothe et al., 2010.

claim: Although a labeled line code for ITD is too inefficient, summing the activity in each hemisphere discards too much of the information that is present in neural activity patterns.
source: Our results demonstrate that, although a labeled line code for ITD—the most literal interpretation of the Jeffress model—is too inefficient, summing the activity in each hemisphere discards too much of the information that is present in neural activity patterns.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: The critical flaw of the hemispheric decoder lies in the fact that an estimate of ITD based on global hemispheric activity is not robust to changes in sound properties other than ITD.
source: The critical flaw lies in the fact that an estimate of ITD based on global hemispheric activity is not robust to changes in sound properties other than ITD.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: Previous studies showing that hemispheric codes for ITD are optimal focused on a simple task, in which only the ITD was allowed to vary.
source: However, these studies focused on a simple task, in which only the ITD was allowed to vary.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous studies.

claim: It is much more difficult to estimate location independently of irrelevant dimensions found in ecological situations, such as level, spectrum, and background noise.
source: It is much more difficult to estimate location independently of irrelevant dimensions found in ecological situations, such as level, spectrum, and background noise.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about sensory estimation.

claim: When the hemispheric decoder is calibrated for broadband sounds and tested with the same sounds as before, performance degrades drastically.
source: However, when the decoder is calibrated for broadband sounds and tested with the same sounds as before, performance degrades drastically (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The results directly demonstrate that indiscriminate pooling of the activity in each hemisphere is a poor way to decode information about sound location.
source: Thus, our results directly demonstrate that indiscriminate pooling of the activity in each hemisphere is a poor way to decode information about sound location.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: Figure 7A directly contradicts the claim that the optimal code for ITD consists of two populations of identically tuned neurons.
source: Figure 7A also directly contradicts the claim that the optimal code for ITD consists of two populations of identically tuned neurons (Harper and McAlpine, 2004).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and contradicts the claim from Harper and McAlpine, 2004.

claim: Heterogeneity of tunings is critical for robust estimation.
source: On the contrary, heterogeneity of tunings is critical for robust estimation, consistently with theoretical arguments (Brette, 2010).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by Figure 7A and citation to Brette, 2010.

claim: The discrepancy with previous arguments in favor of hemispheric or 'slope' coding seems to stem from a confusion between accuracy and acuity.
source: The discrepancy with previous arguments in favor of hemispheric or 'slope' coding seems to stem from a confusion between accuracy and acuity (Heffner and Heffner, 2005; Tollin et al., 2005): accuracy measures how well one can estimate the correct value (absolute localization); acuity measures how easily one can distinguish between two values (discrimination).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the discrepancy with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Acuity can be directly related to ITD sensitivity of neural responses (favoring a 'slope code'), but accuracy is in fact the relevant ecological concept for the animal.
source: Acuity can be directly related to ITD sensitivity of neural responses (favoring a 'slope code'), but accuracy is in fact the relevant ecological concept for the animal.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why previous studies may have reached different conclusions.

claim: For a given level of accuracy, the hemispheric decoder requires many more neurons than the pattern match decoder, and therefore it is energetically inefficient.
source: However, our results also imply that for a given level of accuracy, the hemispheric decoder requires many more neurons than the pattern match decoder (Figures 3A and 6D), and therefore it is energetically inefficient.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3A and 6D.

claim: The structure of neural correlations can be critical to optimal decoding.
source: It is known that the structure of neural correlations can be critical to optimal decoding.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: In the medial superior olive (MSO), correlations due to anatomical divergence are probably limited because frequencies are narrowly tuned in these binaural neurons and receive inputs from few monaural neurons.
source: In the medial superior olive (MSO), the earliest nucleus with ITD-sensitive neurons, correlations due to anatomical divergence are probably limited because frequencies are narrowly tuned in these binaural neurons and receive inputs from few monaural neurons (Couchman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Couchman et al., 2010.

claim: Correlations due to shared variability from feedback or lateral connections are likely to be weak in the MSO because there are no identified lateral connections within the MSO and little evidence of feedback connections.
source: The second source of correlations is also likely to be weak because there are no identified lateral connections within the MSO and little evidence of feedback connections, although GABAergic receptors have been recently characterized (Couchman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Couchman et al., 2012.

claim: Neural correlations in the early sound localization circuit are presumably mainly due to the shared acoustic stimulus.
source: Thus, neural correlations in this early sound localization circuit are presumably mainly due to the shared acoustic stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of correlation sources in the MSO.

claim: When neural correlations are neglected and neurons are assumed to fire independently, conditionally to the ITD, then the optimal code is the most sensitive one.
source: When these correlations are neglected and neurons are assumed to fire independently, conditionally to the ITD, then the optimal code is the most sensitive one (Harper and McAlpine, 2004), and reliable estimates can be obtained by simply pooling the estimates obtained from individual responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harper and McAlpine, 2004.

claim: This conclusion is wrong in general when there are stimulus-dependent correlations.
source: This conclusion is wrong in general when there are stimulus-dependent correlations (Brette, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brette, 2010.

claim: The structure of neural correlations contains useful information that can be exploited by simple decoders.
source: In this case, as we have shown, the structure of neural correlations contains useful information that can be exploited by simple decoders.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the decoder performance analysis.

claim: Changes in various aspects of the sound induce shared variability in individual responses, which results in the same variability in pooled responses, but little variability in the relative activity of neurons (used by the pattern decoder).
source: For example, changes in various aspects of the sound induce shared variability in individual responses, which results in the same variability in pooled responses, but little variability in the relative activity of neurons (used by the pattern decoder).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why the pattern decoder is more robust.

claim: Another mechanism to reduce the impact of shared stimulus-dependent variability is divisive normalization.
source: Another mechanism to reduce the impact of shared stimulus-dependent variability is divisive normalization (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: Level normalization was included in all the models tested.
source: Level normalization was in fact included in all the models we tested, so as to focus on ITD cues (rather than interaural level differences).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model.

claim: Previous studies have assessed the performance of pattern decoders in estimating sound location from the responses of ensembles of cortical neurons.
source: Previous studies have assessed the performance of pattern decoders in estimating sound location from the responses of ensembles of cortical neurons.
evidence: This is stated as background on previous studies.

claim: It is generally found that good performance can be achieved with pattern decoders provided that the set of neurons is large enough.
source: It is generally found that good performance can be achieved provided that the set of neurons is large enough.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous findings.

claim: A previous study found good performance with an opponent channel model, similar to the hemispheric model tested in this study.
source: A previous study also found good performance with an opponent channel model, similar to the hemispheric model we tested in our study (Stecker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stecker et al., 2005.

claim: Previous studies testing pattern decoders tested the decoders on responses to a single type of sound (white noise), although with several levels.
source: However, these studies tested the decoders on responses to a single type of sound (white noise), although with several levels, and as we have shown, substantial differences between the performances of decoding mechanisms only arise when sounds are allowed to vary in dimensions other than the dimension being estimated (e.g., spectrum).
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous studies.

claim: In a recent experimental study, a maximum likelihood decoder was found to outperform a hemispheric decoder in estimating sound location from responses of neurons in the inferior colliculus.
source: In a recent experimental study, a maximum likelihood decoder was found to outperform a hemispheric decoder in estimating sound location from responses of neurons in the inferior colliculus (Day and Delgutte, 2013), which is consistent with our study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Day and Delgutte, 2013.

claim: The pattern decoder is essentially a perceptron: spatially tuned neurons are formed by simply pooling neural responses with different weights, and then the maximally active neuron indicates source location.
source: The pattern decoder is essentially a perceptron (Dayan and Abbott, 2001): spatially tuned neurons are formed by simply pooling neural responses with different weights, and then the maximally active neuron indicates source location.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the pattern decoder, with citation to Dayan and Abbott, 2001.

claim: The weights in the pattern decoder reflect the average activity pattern for the preferred location, and thus could be learned by standard Hebbian plasticity mechanisms.
source: These weights reflect the average activity pattern for the preferred location, and thus could be learned by standard Hebbian plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about how the pattern decoder could be implemented neurally.

claim: The smoothed peak decoder is essentially the same as the pattern decoder, except the weights are not learned.
source: The smoothed peak decoder is essentially the same, except the weights are not learned.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the two decoders.

claim: In the cat model, most low-frequency neurons in the central nucleus of the inferior colliculus are spatially tuned, with preferred azimuth homogeneously distributed in the contralateral hemifield.
source: In the cat model, most low-frequency neurons in the central nucleus of the inferior colliculus are spatially tuned, with preferred azimuth homogeneously distributed in the contralateral hemifield (Aitkin et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aitkin et al., 1985.

claim: Spatially tuned neurons in the inferior colliculus receive excitatory inputs from ITD-sensitive neurons in the MSO.
source: These neurons receive excitatory inputs from ITD-sensitive neurons in the MSO.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about auditory anatomy.

claim: When one inferior colliculus is removed, sound localization performance drops only in the contralateral field.
source: In addition, when one inferior colliculus is removed, sound localization performance drops only in the contralateral field.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from lesion studies.

claim: Both the pattern and smooth peak decoders are in line with the findings that spatially tuned neurons exist in the IC and that unilateral lesions affect only the contralateral field.
source: Both the pattern and smooth peak decoders are in line with these findings.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the compatibility of these decoders with physiological findings.

claim: Contrary to the other decoders, the presence of both functional hemispheres is required for the hemispheric decoder to estimate sound direction in either hemifield.
source: First, contrary to the other decoders, the presence of both functional hemispheres is required to estimate sound direction in either hemifield.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the hemispheric decoder.

claim: The hemispheric decoder produces a graded estimate of sound direction, not a spatially tuned response.
source: Second, these operations produce a graded estimate of sound direction, not a spatially tuned response.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the hemispheric decoder.

claim: Producing spatially tuned responses from the hemispheric decoder requires an additional step, with neurons tuned to a specific ratio of hemispheric activity.
source: Therefore, producing spatially tuned responses requires an additional step, with neurons tuned to a specific ratio of hemispheric activity.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for the hemispheric decoder to produce spatially tuned responses.

claim: The firing rate of neurons that produce spatially tuned responses from hemispheric activity must depend nonmonotonically on the activity of each side.
source: The firing rate of these neurons must then depend nonmonotonically on the activity of each side.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for neurons that produce spatially tuned responses from hemispheric activity.

claim: The hemispheric decoder appears more complex, in terms of neural circuitry, than any of the other decoders.
source: Thus, the hemispheric decoder appears more complex, in terms of neural circuitry, than any of the other decoders.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the complexity of the hemispheric decoder.

claim: There are spatially tuned neurons in the inferior colliculus.
source: However, in addition to the fact that there are spatially tuned neurons in the inferior colliculus (Aitkin et al., 1985), this idea does not fit with what is known of the physiology of eye movements.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aitkin et al., 1985.

claim: Cats orient their gaze toward a briefly presented sound, a behavioral response that has been used to measure sound localization accuracy.
source: Cats orient their gaze toward a briefly presented sound, a behavioral response that has been used to measure sound localization accuracy (Tollin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tollin et al., 2005.

claim: Eye movements are controlled by neurons in the superior colliculus (SC), which form a map (a 'place code').
source: Eye movements are controlled by neurons in the superior colliculus (SC), which form a map (a 'place code'): stimulation of neurons in the SC produces saccades whose amplitude and direction depend on the site of stimulation, but not on intensity or frequency of stimulation (Sparks and Nelson, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sparks and Nelson, 1987.

claim: Some neurons in the superior colliculus are tuned to sound location.
source: Some of these neurons are tuned to sound location (Populin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Populin et al., 2004.

claim: The anatomy and physiology of the ITD processing pathway are very similar across mammalian species.
source: The anatomy and physiology of the ITD processing pathway are very similar across mammalian species (Grothe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grothe et al., 2010.

claim: If there is a common mechanism for ITD processing in mammals, it cannot be based on pooling neural activity on each hemisphere.
source: Therefore, if there is a common mechanism for ITD processing in mammals, it cannot be based on pooling neural activity on each hemisphere.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the inconsistency of the hemispheric decoder with behavioral data in cats and humans.

claim: A traditional argument in favor of the hemispheric model of ITD processing or 'slope coding' is that in small mammals, there are many binaural neurons with large BDs, which is contradictory with a labeled line code.
source: A traditional argument in favor of the hemispheric model of ITD processing or 'slope coding' is that in small mammals, there are many binaural neurons with large BDs, which is contradictory with a labeled line code.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of a traditional argument.

claim: There are many binaural neurons with small BDs (within the ecological range), both in small and large mammals, which is contradictory with the slope coding hypothesis.
source: However, it should be noted that the exact symmetrical argument applies as well: there are many binaural neurons with small BDs (within the ecological range), both in small and large mammals, which is contradictory with the slope coding hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated as a counter-argument to the traditional argument for slope coding.

claim: To understand how ITD is extracted, one must identify those aspects of neural responses that are specific to ITD.
source: To understand how ITD is extracted, one must identify those aspects of neural responses that are specific to ITD.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for understanding neural coding.

claim: One must analyze not only what varies with ITD but also what is invariant when properties other than ITD vary.
source: In other words, one must analyze not only what varies with ITD but also what is invariant when properties other than ITD vary.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for understanding neural coding.

claim: The computationally challenging task for a sensory system is not to discriminate between two signals, but to extract meaningful information in face of the tremendous diversity of sensory inputs in ecological environments.
source: Indeed, the computationally challenging task for a sensory system is not to discriminate between two signals, but to extract meaningful information in face of the tremendous diversity of sensory inputs in ecological environments.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about sensory systems.

claim: The cells are modeled as generalized cross-correlators with an internal delay BD.
source: The cells are then modeled as generalized cross-correlators with an internal delay BD (Yin et al., 1987) (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model, supported by citation to Yin et al., 1987.

claim: The computational model used has been shown to produce realistic responses.
source: We therefore decided to base our comparison on responses generated by a standard computational model, fitted with empirical data, which has been shown to produce realistic responses ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated as justification for using the computational model.

claim: Obtaining 11 hours of sound per cell from electrophysiological recordings is not feasible because it would correspond to more than 7 months of single-unit recordings.
source: Obtaining this amount of data from electrophysiological recordings is not feasible because it would correspond to more than 7 months of single-unit recordings.
evidence: This is stated as justification for using the computational model.

claim: The strongest responses lie along the line of the ITD.
source: The strongest responses lie along the line of the ITD.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 1C.

claim: Smoothing in the smoothed peak decoder could be neurally implemented by pooling the activity of cells with similar tuning.
source: Smoothing could be neurally implemented by pooling the activity of cells with similar tuning.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about neural implementation.

claim: The binaural model is a generalization of two previous models that were found to produce good fits for the delay–response curves of the guinea pig and owl models.
source: This binaural model is a generalization of two previous models that were found to produce good fits for the delay–response curves of the guinea pig (Harper and McAlpine, 2004) and owl models (Fischer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harper and McAlpine, 2004 and Fischer et al., 2008.

claim: The delay–response curves of the generalized model give good fits to published data for the cat.
source: Here, we generalized it to include cats and humans, and checked that the delay–response curves give good fits to published data for the cat (Joris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the model, supported by citation to Joris et al., 2006.

claim: The measured guinea pig HRTFs had a maximal ITD of 250 μs.
source: ITDs were found to be frequency dependent, a maximal ITD of 250 μs, consistent with previously reported measurements in live guinea pigs (Sterbing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the HRTF measurements.

claim: The cat HRTFs had a maximal ITD of 450 μs.
source: For the HRTF model, we used the HRTFs recorded by Tollin and Koka (2009b), which had a maximal ITD of 450 μs.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the cat HRTFs used.

claim: The barn owl HRTFs had a maximal ITD of 260 μs.
source: We used HRTFs and a distribution of BDs measured from barn owl IC from Wagner et al. (2007). BDs were chosen using the same procedure as in cats, with KDE estimates. The HRTFs had a maximal ITD of 260 μs.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the owl HRTFs used, supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2007.

claim: The owl is known to be ITD sensitive above 2 kHz.
source: BFs from 2–8 kHz were used, as the owl is known to be ITD sensitive above 2 kHz (Coles and Guppy, 1988), and the HRTFs were only accurate up to 8 kHz.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coles and Guppy, 1988.

claim: The human HRTFs had a maximal ITD of approximately 950 μs.
source: HRTFs from the IRCAM LISTEN database (http://www.ircam.fr/equipes/salles/listen/) were used. These had a maximal ITD of approximately 950 μs.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the human HRTFs used.
